issues.legal_issue: The High Court cannot use its constitutional writ or supervisory powers to quash a plaint in a civil suit.
material_facts: A petition asked the High Court to quash a plaint and proceedings in a civil suit concerning a shop and the parties’ competing claims to it.
The High Court quashed the plaint and further proceedings, but the Supreme Court held that constitutional writ or supervisory powers cannot be exercised to question a plaint.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not competent to quash the plaint through the proceedings before it, and its judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Shalini Shyam Shetty v. Rajendra Shankar Patil, (2010) 8 SCC 329, concerning the limits on writ intervention in private landlord-tenant disputes, and Jai Singh v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi, (2010) 9 SCC 385, concerning the careful and constrained exercise of supervisory jurisdiction. It held that if a suit is not maintainable, that question may be decided in appropriate proceedings, but Articles 226 and 227 cannot be used to question a plaint.

predicates.constitutional_petition_seeks_to_quash_c: A person asks a constitutional court to set aside a plaint filed in a subordinate civil court.
predicates.constitutional_court_cannot_quash_civil_: The constitutional court does not use its writ or supervisory powers to set aside a civil plaint.

issues.definition: When a constitutional petition seeks to quash a civil plaint, the rule bars the constitutional court from quashing it through those powers.

issues.legal_issue: Constitutional writ or supervisory jurisdiction cannot be used to decide a private landlord-tenant dispute or an intensely disputed factual question about alleged harassment when no excess of jurisdiction by the subordinate court is alleged.
material_facts: The dispute involved competing claims concerning occupation and ownership of a shop, including an asserted landlord-tenant relationship.
The respondent alleged that the appellant had obtained court orders against another person deceitfully to harass the respondent and close the respondent’s business.
Whether the orders were obtained with an intent to harass was a factual issue; no issue had been framed and no evidence had been produced to establish that allegation.
The respondent was not a party to the suits in which the challenged orders were made and could have challenged those orders before an appropriate forum.
The respondent did not contend that the subordinate court had acted without jurisdiction or exceeded its jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not entertain the petition to determine the private dispute or the disputed allegation of harassment; its judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226, a petition cannot be used to determine a landlord-tenant dispute or an intense dispute between private individuals. Under Article 227, as explained in Jai Singh v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi, (2010) 9 SCC 385, supervisory jurisdiction ensures that subordinate courts act within the bounds of their authority; it is exercised with care and is not a general means of correcting errors by courts acting within their jurisdiction. Shalini Shyam Shetty v. Rajendra Shankar Patil, (2010) 8 SCC 329, was relied on for the limits on writ intervention in private landlord-tenant disputes.

predicates.constitutional_petition_concerns_private: A person brings a constitutional petition seeking relief concerning a dispute between private individuals.
predicates.landlord_tenant_dispute: The private dispute concerns the parties’ asserted landlord-tenant relationship or occupation of rented premises.
predicates.intensely_disputed_harassment_facts: A party alleges harassment or improper purpose, and deciding the allegation requires resolving disputed facts.
predicates.subordinate_court_jurisdictional_excess_: The petitioner alleges that the subordinate court acted without jurisdiction or beyond the limits of its jurisdiction.
predicates.constitutional_court_cannot_use_writ_or_: The constitutional court does not use writ or supervisory jurisdiction to decide the private dispute or resolve its disputed factual allegations.

issues.definition: When a constitutional petition concerns a private dispute involving a landlord-tenant relationship or intensely disputed harassment facts, and no jurisdictional excess by the subordinate court is alleged, the constitutional court cannot use writ or supervisory jurisdiction to determine that dispute.
